name: Artificial Intelligence Act
evidence_rating: forecasts only: main obligations not yet applicable (postponed to 2027-28); no ex-post evidence; ex-ante cost assumptions contested
summary: The AI Act's main high-risk obligations do not yet apply and were postponed in 2026 to December 2027 and August 2028, so its effects cannot yet be measured. One of its own success indicators - the share of firms using AI - rose from 8% (2023) to 20% (2025), but this reflects the generative-AI boom rather than the Act. The Commission's forecast of EUR 100-500m compliance costs assumed only 5-15% of AI systems would be high-risk; start-up surveys put that share at 33-50%.

indicators.objective: Ensure AI systems placed on the market and used are safe and respect fundamental rights and Union values
Ensure legal certainty to facilitate investment and innovation in AI
Enhance governance and effective enforcement of existing law on fundamental rights and safety
Facilitate a single market for lawful, safe and trustworthy AI and prevent fragmentation

indicators.indicator: Number of serious incidents or breaches of fundamental-rights obligations (semi-annual), by field, absolute and relative
indicators.evidence: Not yet reportable: high-risk obligations not yet applicable; the 2026 AI omnibus postponed them to 2 Dec 2027 (Annex III) and 2 Aug 2028 (Annex I).

indicators.indicator: Total AI investment in the EU and by Member State (annual)
indicators.evidence: No Commission series linked to the Act found yet.

indicators.indicator: Share of companies using AI (annual) / share of SMEs using AI
indicators.evidence: Measurable via Eurostat: 7.7% (2021), 8.1% (2023), 13.5% (2024), about 20% (2025) of EU enterprises with 10+ staff; 55% of large firms in 2025. Rise cannot be attributed to the Act (main obligations not yet applicable; generative-AI boom).

indicators.indicator: Aggregate compliance cost EUR 100-500m by 2025 (up to 4-5% of high-risk AI investment) plus verification 2-5%; high-risk = 5-15% of AI applications
indicators.evidence: Not evaluated. Start-up surveys put the high-risk share at 33-50% of their systems, far above the 5-15% assumed; obligations later postponed and simplified.

literature.citation: European Commission (2021), Impact Assessment accompanying the AI Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2021) 85), SWD(2021) 84
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the AI Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2021) 85)
literature.headline: Aggregate compliance cost EUR 100-500m by 2025 (up to 4-5% of investment in high-risk AI, assumed 5-15% of applications), plus 2-5% verification costs; SMEs expected to benefit from higher trust
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected compliance to cost EUR 100-500 million in total by 2025, because only 5-15% of AI systems would count as high-risk.

literature.citation: Eurostat (2025), Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises, Statistics Explained (data extracted December 2025)
literature.title: Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises
literature.headline: AI use by EU enterprises (10+ employees): 7.7% (2021), 8.1% (2023), 13.5% (2024), 19.95% (2025); large enterprises 55%; Denmark 42%, Romania 5%
literature.summary_plain: One in five EU firms used AI in 2025, up from one in thirteen in 2023 - one of the Act's own success indicators, though the rise reflects the generative-AI boom rather than the Act.

literature.citation: Council of the EU / European Parliament (2026), Digital Omnibus on AI (amending the AI Act): postponement of high-risk obligations, Political agreement 7 May 2026; Parliament 16 June, Council 29 June 2026
literature.authors: Council of the EU / European Parliament
literature.title: Digital Omnibus on AI (amending the AI Act): postponement of high-risk obligations
literature.venue: Political agreement 7 May 2026; Parliament 16 June, Council 29 June 2026
literature.headline: High-risk obligations postponed from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027 (Annex III) and from 2 Aug 2027 to 2 Aug 2028 (Annex I)
literature.summary_plain: Two years after adoption, EU lawmakers postponed the AI Act's main high-risk rules by more than a year to give firms and standard-setters more time.
literature.quality: law-firm summary; check Official Journal text

literature.citation: appliedAI Institute / Digital Poland et al. (2022), AI Act Impact Survey: Exploring the impact of the AI Act on startups in Europe, Survey of 113 AI start-ups and VC firms
literature.authors: appliedAI Institute / Digital Poland et al.
literature.title: AI Act Impact Survey: Exploring the impact of the AI Act on startups in Europe
literature.venue: Survey of 113 AI start-ups and VC firms
literature.headline: 33-50% of start-ups expected their systems to be high-risk (vs 5-15% assumed by the Commission); about 16% considered stopping AI development or relocating outside the EU; 73% of surveyed VCs expected reduced competitiveness
literature.summary_plain: Before adoption, many AI start-ups expected far more of their products to be classed as high-risk than the Commission assumed, and some considered leaving the EU.
literature.quality: small, self-selected sample; expectations not outcomes
